title: Anatomy of a Denial Letter — Estate of Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group
description: A 91-year-old man's own physical therapist documented he could barely move. The algorithm that decided his care cut it off anyway. Sourced from the filed federal class-action complaint, Estate of Gene B. Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group, Case No. 0:23-cv-03514 (D. Minn.).
sourceCitation: Estate of Gene B. Lokken, et al. v. UnitedHealth Group, Inc., et al., Case No. 0:23-cv-03514, U.S. District Court, District of Minnesota, filed 11/14/2023. This is an active lawsuit — the allegations described have not been proven in court. All quoted language is sourced directly from the filed Class Action Complaint, a public court record. This video uses AI-generated narration. Educational content only, not legal or medical advice.

scenes.narrationText: He fell. He broke his leg and his ankle. He was 91 years old. Thirteen days into physical therapy, this is the letter he got.
Case file zero-zero-four. UnitedHealth Group. A real federal lawsuit. Filed by a real family.
This is the actual language from his denial notice, quoted word for word in the federal complaint. "More inpatient days at the skilled nursing facility are not medically necessary.
A safe discharge plan has been recommended." That's it. That's the entire stated reason. No explanation of what changed. No reference to his actual condition.

find.text: A safe discharge plan has been recommended

scenes.narrationText: Here's what his own physical therapist wrote in his chart, the same week: "Neuromuscular: decreased movement and mobility. Musculoskeletal: paralysis, weakness." One document says he was ready to go home. The other says he could barely move. According to the lawsuit, both were true — but only one of them was written by a person who ever saw him.

The lawsuit alleges the actual decision-maker wasn't a doctor. It was an algorithm called nH Predict — built by a UnitedHealth subsidiary, comparing him against a database of six million other patients to estimate how much care he "should" need.

visual.label: PATIENT RECORDS THE ALGORITHM COMPARED HIM AGAINST

scenes.narrationText: According to the complaint, roughly ninety percent of denials like his are overturned on appeal. That's not a rounding error. That's a machine getting it wrong nine times out of ten — and still being used to make the first call.

visual.label: OF DENIALS LIKE HIS ARE OVERTURNED ON APPEAL

scenes.narrationText: His family appealed. Twice. According to the complaint, coverage was never reinstated. They paid twelve to fourteen thousand dollars a month, out of pocket, to keep him in care. Mr. Lokken remained in that facility until he passed away in July 2023. This lawsuit is still active — nothing here has been decided by a court yet.

If your own denial letter reads like a form response — a short, generic phrase with no specific detail about your case — that's worth noticing. You have the right to ask, in writing, whose clinical judgment made the decision, and what records they actually reviewed.

visual.text:
Ask in writing: "What clinical record
was reviewed, and by whom?"
